appraisal_events.evidence: Walking « assez difficilement à cause des blessures », the baron displays before « ce harem qui semblait presque l'intimider » the « hochements de taille et de tête » of someone wishing « de paraître grande dame » in « un milieu inférieur »; he greets a gigolo « comme il eût salué un prince à Versailles », talks a borrowed argot, and is finally « désespéré et exaspéré par cet effort factice vers la perversité », paying Maurice « de l'air dépité de quelqu'un qu'on a floué ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator lowers Charlus twice over in the same movement: by exposing the coquettish, would-be great-lady performance he puts on for hired boys, and by showing his purchased fantasy dissolve against their commonplace decency.

appraisal_events.evidence: « C'est tout le contraire de ce que tu m'as dit », the baron tells him of the boy sold to him as an assassin; Jupien, « pris au dépourvu », can only object that the young man is on bad terms with his father — « évidemment faible comme crime auprès de l'assassinat » — and his excuse (« vous êtes trop naïf ») ends by « ne faisant que froisser l'amour-propre de M. de Charlus ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Jupien is reproached by his patron for a piece of stage-management that failed and makes his position worse with every reply, the narration marking each of his answers as inadequate.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Comme il est simple ! jamais on ne dirait un prince », say some of the habitués once M. de Charlus has gone out, escorted downstairs by Jupien.
appraisal_events.explanation: Within the house his rank is registered and admired: the clients credit him with a princely quality worn lightly. The narration ironizes the compliment by placing it immediately after the scene it rewards and beside the dead man whose title nobody there could name.

appraisal_events.evidence: The house mourns a dead client of whom the gigolos say « Je ne sais pas son nom, il paraît que c'est un baron » and who « n'était autre que le prince de Foix »: « Passant, chez sa femme, pour vivre beaucoup au cercle, en réalité il passait des heures chez Jupien à bavarder, à raconter des histoires du monde devant des voyous. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator posthumously unmasks a second aristocrat, whose supposed life at the club was spent entertaining hoodlums in a brothel and whose very name and rank were unknown to the people who regret him.

status_effects.explanation: The passage's verdict on him is severe: preening for hired boys, faking their language, and cheated of the vice he has paid for.

Inside the establishment his rank is spoken of with admiration — he passes for a prince whose simplicity is remarked on — which locally raises him in that milieu even as everything around the remark undercuts it.
Caught out by the baron's reproach, he improvises a feeble substitute crime and an excuse that only offends his patron further.
The narrator's disclosure reduces him to a double life conducted before hoodlums who did not even know who he was, and extends the doubt to his surveillance of his son.

ambiguities: « prince de Foix » here designates the dead father, whom the passage distinguishes from « le jeune prince de Foix », l'ami de Saint-Loup, who bears the same name; the entity is not on the reference sheet and is left unresolved.

The habitués' compliment (« jamais on ne dirait un prince ») is a genuine local elevation but is voiced by men who have just flogged him and reported in the same breath as their ignorance of the prince de Foix's name, so its evaluative weight is deliberately unstable.
